prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian prose grounded in a poet's language, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical imaginative architecture of rare scale and formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu, one writer in one prize part. The reasons are literary, and I do not count the convergence of opening rankings as one. Voice: the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, as I know them from public knowledge and translation, are recognizable as no one else's. Formal and linguistic achievement: the patterning is carried by the sentence and by the large architecture together. Depth: memory, the body and metaphysical speculation form one project, not a collection of effects. Sustained quality: the work begins in poetry and moves into long prose cycles, and later books appear to extend earlier ones. That is an arc, not a single peak. Round 1 showed me that I was treating the poetic strand as better supported than the evidence allows. I said I would want the poetry examined directly, and no colleague has supplied that examination. I therefore narrow the citation. It now names a prose achievement grounded in a poet's language, not poetry and prose as two co-equal strands. This answers the chair's question on citation scope. It rests on what the committee can actually assess, and it makes no claim the thin translated poetry cannot support. Attribution is unambiguous. The configuration is one name in one prize part, and I do not prefer P000.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains translation. Much of the claim lies in Romanian sentence rhythm and density, which I can judge only through translations of varying quality and through public accounts. The second reservation is that length and elaboration may become repetition in some volumes, and public knowledge cannot settle whether the later work extends the earlier. The third is that I have not directly examined the poetry and early work, for example the early prose such as Nostalgia and the long poem Levantul as I know them from public record. The poetic ground I cite in the citation is therefore partly inferred. Finally, my scholarly interests (modern poetry, the fragment, nihilism and mysticism) are context only. They are a standing reason to ask whether I overvalue an inward, metaphysical project. Round 1 produced no evidence of such bias, but also none that excludes it.

responses.point: Carlberg argued that translation limits are shared by Cărtărescu, Adonis and Can Xue and should not be applied unevenly. She said she sees no principled basis for ranking Can Xue as low as eighth, and she would want evidence of development across the corpus before putting Can Xue above Adonis.
responses.response: She is right, and I accept the correction. My eighth place for Can Xue partly reflected a translation doubt that applies equally to Adonis, and I treated it as heavier for her than for him. I still hold that the Cărtărescu case is more readable in translation, because large-scale architecture survives translation better than prosody does. That is a difference of degree, not a licence to ignore Can Xue. Where we still differ is the order of the alternatives. I keep Adonis ahead of her in my own list because I rate the formal case for the renewal of Arabic poetic language highly. But I move Can Xue into my second alternative slot, replacing Carson, because the round 1 exchange showed me that my last-place ranking was too severe. I agree that an Adonis citation must be confined to the poetry. Like her, I rely on secondary accounts for it, so I rank it below a case I can argue from structure.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argued that Can Xue's dream-logic fiction is unlike other Chinese-language fiction, that this distinctiveness deserves more weight than a last-place ranking gives it, and that translation limits are the committee's own reading problem and should not count against her. He also questioned how a non-Arabic reader can assess the central claim for Adonis.
responses.response: I accept the first part. Distinctiveness of voice is a stated criterion, and I should not let an open question about development erase it. My remaining doubt is narrower: I do not know whether the method deepens or recurs, and I cannot answer that from the translated sample. But I agree that this is a question about our evidence, not a verdict on her. On Adonis, your question is the right one and I cannot fully answer it. I can say what a non-Arabic reader can reasonably weigh: the structural moves visible in translation, such as myth, fragmentation and the dialogue with inherited forms, and the accounts of Arabic readers. The prosodic core cannot be tested by us. This is why I keep him as an alternative and not as my first choice, and why anonymous regional expert reports on Arabic poetry, if available to the committee, would carry weight. I cannot establish what any such report says.

responses.point: Mattson named the risk that length and elaboration shade into repetition. She said Cărtărescu's cycles are cumulative in scale and register, and that the poetry-to-prose arc gives more evidence of development than Can Xue's method does. She also said Michon is a strong second-tier case, not a first choice, because of corpus size.
responses.response: I agree that repetition is the decisive risk, and I take your test as the right one: whether later volumes bring new formal solutions or only new quantities of the same material. I cannot confirm this volume by volume, and I will not claim to. I do think the round 1 files give a reasonable basis for a provisional judgment, since nobody has produced concrete evidence of exhaustion and several members describe extension. That judgment is provisional, and I would revise it if a colleague who knows the late work showed otherwise. On Michon, I agree that a small corpus is not disqualifying, but that for me his case rests too heavily on sentence-level style, which translation conveys least. I would not move him into my alternatives.

responses.point: Palm described Cărtărescu's major works as an integrated body and not isolated peaks. She leans toward reading recurrence as architectural principle but calls it a judgment, not a verified fact. In her response to me she also attributed to me a question about how far Zurita's page-based poetry holds up apart from the memorial and landscape gestures.
responses.response: I accept the integration point, and it supports the whole-oeuvre reading that I find strongest. I also share her caution that it is a judgment. I must correct the record on Zurita, as the chair summary notes. I ranked Zurita fourth in my opening, but my round 1 file does not state the question about page-based poetry that she attributes to me. The question is reasonable, and it is a fair one to put to any poet whose work includes landscape-scale interventions. It is not a position I put in my file, and I will not claim it retroactively. I would rank him below my first three alternatives for reasons unrelated to that question. Poetry is the genre most damaged by translation, and I have too little direct evidence to move him up.

responses.point: Sward holds Carson as an alternative while saying the hardest part is the citation scope, since scholarly and translation components are difficult to weigh against the poetry. She argued that inventiveness and intellectual depth, not volume, should be the whole-oeuvre test, and she is unpersuaded that Jorge should lead.
responses.response: I agree that inventiveness and depth, not volume, are the right test, and I have applied it to Carson, whom I ranked third. The citation problem is what keeps her from my first alternative slot. A citation for hybrid forms that sit between scholarship, lyric and drama would have to be narrow, and I doubt it can name a whole oeuvre without either stretching the category or leaving out much of the work. I would not call that a barrier. It is a difficulty of the kind that arose for Cărtărescu's poetic strand, and it should be decided the same way, by naming only what the committee can actually assess. On Jorge, I share your hesitation about singularity of voice and have not been moved by round 1. Palm has not yet named the passages or devices that would show a voice distinct from other historical novelists.

uncertainties: Translation: how far the Romanian sentence rhythm and density of Cărtărescu's prose survive in the available translations is unresolved. The same limit applies, probably more strongly, to the prosody of Adonis and to the Chinese prose of Can Xue.
Corpus coverage: the poetry and early work of Cărtărescu are thinly visible in translation. The poetic ground named in the citation is partly inferred, and I have not examined it directly.

Maturity: whether the metaphysical density is sustained and extended across the whole corpus, or repeats motifs in some volumes, cannot be settled from public knowledge. I would revise my view if a colleague who knows the late work showed repetition.
Can Xue: it is unresolved whether her method deepens across decades or recurs, and how representative the translated part of her large output is.
I rely on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions. I have not independently verified any text or read the full corpus in any language.
I cannot establish whether anonymous regional expert reports bear on candidates writing in Arabic, Chinese or Japanese, or what they say.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile. The listed connections (Horace Engdahl, Daniel Birnbaum, the Kris circle, and my scholarly work on Ekelöf, Celan, exile literature and the fragment) show no link to Cărtărescu or to any other shortlisted writer. My scholarly interests are context, not evidence of preference. As chair I wrote the round 1 summary and ranked B014 first myself, so that summary is a record of positions, not a ruling. I also note the chair summary's disclosure that some round 1 responses attributed positions to colleagues that those colleagues' files do not contain. I have corrected the Zurita attribution to me above and do not adjudicate the others.
